messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ibrahim, a 37-year-old firefighter with deep brown eyes and a warm smile, found his life irrevocably altered by a traumatic experience that began two years prior. While returning home from a late shift, he had noticed a figure on a bicycle persistently following him. The unnerving sensation of being tracked settled deep within him as he quickened his pace. What began as a mere inconvenience escalated into a harrowing ordeal that left him feeling vulnerable and exposed. After weeks of being stalked, he felt the weight of fear suffocating him, and the stalking culminated in a confrontation that shattered his sense of safety. Though he had managed to escape physically unharmed, the emotional scars ran deep.

Since that day, Ibrahim's life had become consumed by a series of triggers that haunted him daily. The sight of bicycles brought a rush of anxiety, compelling him to relive memories he wished to forget. Each time he saw a bicycle, the vivid recollections of being followed flooded back, as if the past were unfolding in real time, tightening the grip of fear around his chest. In his mind, the image of the stalker was forever imprinted, and he could feel the old panic rising as he passed a bicycle parked outside his workplace. He found himself scanning every room he entered, searching for exits and assessing potential threats. Even the most innocuous sounds—like a car honking or people laughing nearby—sent him into a state of heightened alertness, the echoes of past fear reverberating in his mind. He felt trapped, as if the world had become an arena full of potential dangers.

As memories of the stalking replayed in his thoughts, the emotional tide would often become too overwhelming for Ibrahim. He would feel an all-consuming wave of anxiety that left him breathless, forcing him to pause and step away from conversations or tasks. In those moments, the resurfacing memories amplified his negative self-view, leading him to believe he was not only reliving the trauma but also proving to himself that he was incapable of coping. It was during these moments that he struggled to articulate what he had experienced; the words eluded him. He had come to believe that his inability to express himself meant he was losing grip on reality, and he feared that he was spiraling into madness. The thought of going crazy loomed over him, amplifying his sense of weakness, making him feel like a diminished version of the man he once was. This internal narrative fed into his memories, making them feel like proof of his inadequacy, as if the trauma had not only changed his reality but also irrevocably altered who he was at his core.

This negative self-view intensified the threats he perceived around him. With every day that passed, he felt more and more convinced that he had been irreparably damaged by the ordeal. The belief that he was weak seeped into his interactions, making him hesitant to engage with colleagues or friends, as if any vulnerability might expose him further. This conviction that he was damaged made him perceive threats everywhere, leading him to view the most benign situations as potential dangers, intensifying his sense of vulnerability. Each time he recoiled from a social situation or avoided a crowded space, it reinforced his internal narrative of inadequacy, further entwining his sense of threat with his self-worth.

Ibrahim's mind became a battleground of conflicting thoughts. He would sometimes catch himself wishing for the ability to forget, to wipe the slate clean of the fear and anxiety that had taken root in his daily life. But the memories of that fateful day were inescapable, often triggered by seemingly innocuous events—the sound of a bicycle bell, a sudden shout, or even the laughter of children playing outside. Each instance would hurl him back into a state of distress, as vivid images of being stalked returned without warning. The memories, once a distant shadow, now loomed large, intertwining with the threat he perceived around him and reinforcing his belief in his own fragility. As these memories took hold, they heightened his sense of threat, leading him to feel as though the danger was not simply past but still very much alive within him.

As he began to navigate his way through these tangled emotions, the weight of his experience became unbearable. He had hoped that time would heal the wounds, but instead, they felt as fresh as ever. Finally, after months of struggling silently, Ibrahim made the courageous decision to seek help. The idea of discussing his trauma filled him with dread, yet he also felt a flicker of hope. What he feared most was that the darkness would swallow him whole, but he also yearned for the day when he could ride his bicycle without looking over his shoulder, when the sound of laughter would no longer send him spiraling into fear. In this moment of vulnerability, he stepped into the therapy room, ready to confront the shadows that had haunted him for far too long. These memories became more vivid and harder to push away, as he internalized the belief that he should have been able to prevent what happened, reinforcing his focus on the trauma each time it resurfaced. This constant sense of danger reinforced his belief that he would never be whole again, leading him to conclude that he was fundamentally broken and unworthy of safety.

violation_explanations: There is no causal connection established between Triggers and Memory; while triggers are mentioned, the influence on memories is not clearly articulated.
There is no causal connection established between Triggers and Negative Appraisals; the triggers do not explicitly lead to negative self-beliefs in the text.
There is no causal connection established between Negative Appraisals and Threat; negative beliefs do not directly lead to perceived threats in the vignette.
There is no causal connection established between Negative Appraisals and Memory; negative beliefs do not influence the memories described.
There is no causal connection established between Negative Appraisals and Triggers; negative beliefs do not lead to further triggers in the narrative.
There is no causal connection established between Memory and Threat; memories do not directly lead to a heightened sense of threat in the text.
There is no causal connection established between Memory and Negative Appraisals; memories do not influence negative self-perceptions in the vignette.
There is no causal connection established between Memory and Triggers; memories do not lead to the re-experiencing of triggers in the narrative.
There is no causal connection established between Threat and Negative Appraisals; perceived threats do not directly influence negative beliefs in the text.
